name: Start here: The Innovation Skills Accelerator
content:
👋 Thank you for signing up to participate in the Innovation Skills Accelerator.

👥 Before you begin, please take a moment to review your learner profile and make sure to update your first and last name as you'd like it to appear in your profile and course completion certificate. You can review and update your details by clicking this link.

💡 This introductory online course will provide you with the digital, data and innovation skills to deliver more effective, equitable and engaged policies and services.

👩‍🎓Through videos, self-assessments and worksheets, you will engage in practical lessons learned about improved ways of working.

🕐 The course will be released in three parts and the first part of the course is available for you to start learning. The other two will be released in separate phases that you will be notified of. 

📖 The course consists of 15 modules, which include short videos, optional readings and videos led by expert faculty members in their respective fields.  

🗓️ You can participate in this course at your own pace and on your own schedule.

✅ If you complete the course you will receive a Certificate of Completion, which may be applied to state learning requirements. 

📝 Help us get to know you! Don’t forget to fill out our pre-course survey before you start learning!

Got questions? Email us at hello@innovate-us.org!


Click this link to start the pre-course survey and begin the course!

The Innovation Skills Accelerator is based on "Solving Public Problems: A Practical Guide to Fix Our Government and Change Our World",  (Yale University Press 2021) by Professor Beth Simone Noveck.

content:
• 📖 Move fast and fix things: How to be a public entrepreneur [Opens in a new window], Rowan Conway, Luke Timmons, Ian Burbidge, RSA Lab, July 24, 2018 (Chapters 1 and 2)

    This report describes the findings from a six-month inquiry into applying the “think like a system, act like an entrepreneur” mentality to the challenges of procuring and scaling innovation through government. Through qualitative workshops, deep dives into case studies around the UK and a global practice review, the authors unearthed examples where practitioners have acted entrepreneurially to enable the success of enterprise innovations.

  • 📖 7 skills you need if you want to solve public problems [Opens in a new window], Beth Simone Noveck, Fast Company, June 24, 2021

    This article, which draws from author Beck Noveck’s book, “Solving Public Problems: A Practical Guide to Fix Our Government and Change Our World,” explains the seven skills public problem solvers need to develop in order to change policy to improve people’s lives.

content:
• 📖  Defining and Analyzing the Problem, Jenette Nagy, Chapter 17 in Analyzing Community Problems and Designing and Adapting Community Interventions. Community Tool Box

    In the “Defining and Analyzing the Problem” section of the Community Toolbox, readers will learn how to determine the nature of a problem, clarify the problem, decide to solve the problem, and analyze the problem with our processes. The toolkit includes readings, a checklist, examples, tools, and a PowerPoint presentation to reinforce the learnings on problem definition.

  • 📖  Are You Solving the Right Problems? Responsibly - Volume 1: Mirror, Mirror, Thomas Wedell-Wedellsborg, Harvard Business Review, January-February 2017

    Through over a decade of research into innovation, Thomas Wedell-Wedellsborg found that leaders of private and public sector organizations routinely struggle not with solving problems, but with figuring out what the problems are. In this article, the author outlines seven practices for effective reframing, which can ultimately lead to more creative solutions to the problems themselves.

content:
Universal Methods of Design  

Bella Martin + Bruce Hanington 

125 Methods and approaches, organized and cataloged so you can understand methods, get references for further reading, and see case studies. It’s a great reference. 


The Field Guide to Human Centered Design. 

The classic IDEO guide to HCD. Lots of case studies, examples, as well as How To. The Guide can be downloaded or used online.


Observatory of Public Sector Innovation 

The OECD’s innovation in government website. It says, in About Us: “Turn the new into the normal. We equip governments and public servants with fresh insights, knowledge, tools, and connections to help them explore new possibilities.” There are lots of frameworks and case studies from around the world. 


Transform with Design 

edited by Jochen Schwietzer, Sihem Benmahmoud-Jouni, Sebastian Fixon

Stories of how people implemented HCD in various organizations, from large corporations to health care institutions and government. (Shameless promotion: This book has a chapter about Virginia Hamilton).

Hack Your Bureaucracy: Get Things Done No Matter What Your Role on Any Team 

Marina Nitse and Nick Sinai  

Not a book about HCD per se, but an important book about getting things done in a government setting, focusing on innovation and creating a modern government.

Recoding America: Why Government Is Failing in the Digital Age and How We Can Do Better

Recoding America: Why Government Is Failing in the Digital Age and How We Can Do Better

Jennifer Pahlka

A description of how government has fallen behind, the issues and problems inherent in government agencies, and examples of how innovation can happen within the constraints of bureaucracies.

Problem Framing


What’s Your Problem? Thomas Wedell-Wedellsborg

This terrific book introduces a method for framing and reframing problems. It has many examples, activities, and visual prompts to help you ensure you are anchoring on the right problem. 


Abstraction Ladder 

Luma Institute’s description of how to use the Abstraction Ladder when looking at a problem, to use various lenses before landing on the right problem. 


The 5 Whys 

A good article about the origin and ways to use the 5 Whys process.


Stakeholder Mapping


Stakeholder Mapping 

The Interaction Design Foundation’s article and video about how to create and use a stakeholder map. 


Stakeholder Map 

Civic Makers’ tool for stakeholder mapping, both available as a PDF and as a template in Mural


Asset Mapping UCLA Center for Health Policy Research

This is an older document (it mentions Mapquest), but very good at the hows and whys of asset mapping in a community. This is within the healthcare context and is very relevant to government. 


Empathy Interviews


Empathy FieldGuide Stanford d. school

A practical and useful guide to help you plan customer research, from empathy interviews to observation.


Conduct Empathy Interviews The Learning Accelerator

A well-designed guide to conducting empathy interviews, with other links and sources to explore.  


Journey Mapping


Draw Toast Tom Wujak

It's a great video to kick off a journey mapping activity. Wujak uses the process of drawing toast to describe the process of mapping a process.

name: Resources: News Outlets
content:
Finding solutions from news outlets

News items can often be a way to begin learning about solutions. Solutions or constructive journalism news outlets, in particular, focus specifically on solutions and things that are going right.

Solutions Journalism News Outlets

  • Solutions Journalism Network

    • A key organization dedicated to promoting and providing resources for solutions journalism, offering a database of solutions-focused articles.  That database, the Solutions Story Tracker, pulls, summarizes, tags and links to stories from 2,000 different news outlets. 

  • The New York Times - Headway Section

    • A section focusing on exploring what can be done about the biggest challenges facing society and the innovations that aim to move the world forward.

  • The Philadelphia Citizen

    • A publication that offers news and solutions-driven stories focused on Philadelphia, aiming to engage citizens in solving the city's challenges.

  • Yes! Magazine

    • This publication focuses on optimistic storytelling, covering peace, justice, and sustainability issues with a solutions-oriented approach.

  • Positive News

    • A magazine and online platform based in the UK that emphasizes constructive journalism, showcasing positive developments around the globe.

  • The Christian Science Monitor

    • Offers a "Making a Difference" section among its coverage, focusing on solutions and positive outcomes to various challenges.

  • The Upside (from The Guardian)

    • Dedicated to positive news, The Guardian's Upside section reports on innovations and solutions addressing global issues.

  • The Hechinger Report

    • Specializes in education, exploring solutions to problems across the education system, from early childhood to higher education.

  • CityLab

    • Compiles ideas and solutions from around the world that are focused on city-level problems.

Topic Searching 

  • Google News 

    • A news aggregator that enables you to search across a variety of publications.

  • Google Alerts

    • Enables you to receive an email when new results for a topic you have defined shows up in Google Search.

name: Resources: Academic Research
content:
Finding solutions in academic research Academic research often offers discussions backed by evidence about policy interventions or programs. The challenge is that many journal articles are behind a paywall and can be hard to access without a university login. Here we have listed some aggregators of journal articles that are free to search. We have also included examples of other resources that can similarly lead you to the evidence related to solutions of interest to you.

Academic journal aggregators

  • Social Science Research Network (SSRN)

    SSRN is a searchable online library used to share scholarly research. It covers disciplines that include the applied sciences, health sciences, humanities, life sciences, physical sciences, and social sciences. Most papers can be downloaded free of charge.

  • arXiv.org

    Operated by Cornell University, arXiv.org hosts more than two million scholarly articles in the fields of physics, mathematics, computer science, quantitative biology, quantitative finance, statistics, electrical engineering and systems science, and economics. 

  • ScienceDirect

    Papers published on ScienceDirect focus on scientific, technical and health research, with more than 1.4 million articles freely available to read. Accessing the full database requires subscription, or access through an institution such as a university.

  • Google Scholar

    Google Scholar is a free web search engine that indexes a vast array of scholarly research, including journal articles, conference papers, theses and books. Citation data enables you to explore related research and can help you to assess the value of the research contributions.

  • Connected Papers

    Connected Papers creates visual graphs of related research papers. After entering information about one paper, Connected Papers will map its links to other papers. It can be useful for building your understanding of a new field and help you to explore research that has clustered around a specific topic.


Further resources

  • Google Books

    Searching within Google Books will provide a list of books that match your search terms. In many cases you will be able to access a preview of the book as well as be able to find information about where you can borrow or buy the book.

  • Library of Congress

    The Library of Congress is the largest library in the world and the main research arm of the U.S. Congress. It offers a range of general and specialized collections. You can learn more about how to use the Library’s as a research tool here.

    • Other public and university libraries

    All libraries offer free book search, so it can be worth exploring how they can support your fast field scanning. For example, the New York Public Library has a dedicated research catalog, and university library catalogs, such as Harvard’s HOLLIS library system, can be searched to at least identify relevant materials that may be worth exploring further.

name: Resources: Think tanks and NGOs
content:
Finding solutions in academic research Academic research often offers discussions backed by evidence about policy interventions or programs. The challenge is that many journal articles are behind a paywall and can be hard to access without a university login. Here we have listed some aggregators of journal articles that are free to search. We have also included examples of other resources that can similarly lead you to the evidence related to solutions of interest to you.

  • National Governors Association (NGA) Center for Best Practices

    The NGA  Center for Best Practices is a research and development firm that directly serves the nation’s Governors. Its programs cover policy areas that include energy, environment, public health, education, children and families, economic policy and infrastructure.

  • Social Science Research Council (SSRC)

    The SSRC draws on a global network of 250,000 researchers to share evidence-based policy solutions. Content is curated and organized to be accessible to decision-makers through various knowledge platforms and reports. The ‘Measure of America’ platform, for example, summarizes data related to the distribution of well-being in the United States.

  • The Urban Institute

    Founded by President Johnson in 1968, the Urban Institute seeks to offer solutions through economic and social policy research. Urban uses stories, data tools and blogs to make its research accessible. 

  • Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL)

    With a network of more than 900 researchers at universities around the world, J-PAL conducts randomized impact evaluations to help ensure policy directed at addressing poverty is informed by evidence. 

  • Economic Policy Institute (EPI)

    EPI is a non-partisan think tank which focuses on the economic conditions confronted by low and middle income Americans. EPI’s Economic Analysis and Research Network (EARN) partners with local and state-based organizations to research and advocate for policies that improve equity.

    • Also see: Evidence clearinghouses

name: Resources: Tracking other jurisdictions
content:
Finding solutions from other jurisdictions

Organizations that work across various levels of government to promote the adoption and implementation of policies and practices that are grounded in evidence of effectiveness offer many opportunities to find solutions. 

  • Results for America (RFA)

    RFA helps policymakers at all levels of government harness the power of evidence and data to solve the world’s greatest challenges. Their work includes identifying and scaling effective solutions across various policy areas. RFA’s Economic Mobility Catalog focuses on strategies that local leaders can use to improve upward economic mobility for residents.

  • The National Governors Association (NGA)

    NGA is a bipartisan organization of U.S. states' governors. The NGA’s Center for Best Practices develops and shares innovative solutions aimed at improving governance at the state level.

  • The Pew Charitable Trusts

    Through its Results First initiative, Pew helped states identify and invest in programs that had proven to be effective in achieving desired outcomes. The Results First Clearinghouse Database is now operated by Penn State University.

  • What Works Cities (WWC)

    A Bloomberg Philanthropies initiative, What Works Cities helps local governments use data and evidence effectively to tackle pressing challenges and improve residents' lives.

  • The Coalition for Evidence-Based Policy

    Now a part of the Laura and John Arnold Foundation, this coalition works to increase government effectiveness through the use of rigorous evidence about "what works."

  • The Center for Evidence-Based Policy

    A national leader in evidence-based decision making and policy design, the center works with public sector leaders at the federal, state, and local levels to solve problems, improve outcomes, and achieve goals more effectively.

  • The Government Accountability Office (GAO) - Evidence-Based Policymaking Page

    GAO provides Congress, the heads of executive agencies, and the public with timely, fact-based, non-partisan information that can be used to improve government and address a variety of challenges through evidence-based policymaking.

  • The National Academies 

    The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine are private, nonprofit institutions that provide expert advice on pressing challenges facing the nation and world. The Academies aim to inform sound policies and public opinion, and advance the pursuit of science, engineering, and medicine.

  • Congressional Research Service

    The Congressional Research Service (CRS) serves as shared staff to congressional committees and Members of Congress. CRS Reports provides public access to non-partisan research products produced by the CRS for the United States Congress.

name: Resources: Finding solutions from people
content:
Finding solutions from people

Informed people are often the fastest shortcut to learning what has been tried, how it got done, and what is working. Here we have listed some ways you can find knowledgeable people in practitioner networks, academia and on social media. Don’t forget you can prompt genAI to help you find knowledgeable people.

Practitioner networks

People with first-hand experiences of implementing policies or programs similar to those you are involved in are often good sources of knowledge about solutions. While reaching out to individuals in other governments is a logical place to begin, becoming involved in communities of practice can be a good way to continually gain and share knowledge about new and innovative interventions.

Here we have suggested an initial list of networks relevant for state government professionals. Further suggestions can be emailed to hello@innovate-us.org

General

  • National Governors Association (NGA)
  • Council of State Governments (CSG)
  • National Conference of State Legislatures

Healthcare

  • National Academy for State Health Policy
  • National Association of State Emergency Medical Services Officials (NASEMSO)
  • National Association of State Alcohol and Drug Abuse Directors (NASADAD)
  • National Association of State Medicaid Directors (NASMD)

Education and Social Policy

  • National Board for Professional Teaching Standards (NBPTS) Networks
  • Chiefs for Change
  • National Association of Social Workers

Technology and Finance

  • State Science and Technology Institute
  • National Association of State Chief Information Officers (NASCIO)
  • National Association of State Budget Officers (NASBO)
  • National Association of State Procurement Officials (NASPO)

Transport, Environment and Economy

  • American Public Transportation Association (APTA)
  • Environmental Council of the States (ECOS)
  • National Association of State Workforce Agencies (NASWA)
  • Economic Development Administration

Academic and scientific experts

The Scholars Strategy Network has been specifically designed to serve as a source of academic experts interested in talking to policymakers. The Network has more than 1800 researchers in 47 states. Combing through relevant documents identified in research aggregators such as Google Scholar and ScienceDirect - see Finding solutions in academic research - is also a good way to find subject matter experts.

Finding experts through social media and the ‘fediverse’

Both legacy and emerging social media platforms can be searched to find authoritative voices on specific topics. LinkedIn, X (previously Twitter), Instagram, Threads, BlueSky, and Mastodon are just some platforms you can use to find a relevant expert or online community with relevant knowledge. Using a hashtag search engine such as Hashtagify can help to identify people who cluster around the specific topic you are most interested in.

Short for ‘federated universe’ the ‘fediverse’ is a series of interconnected networks that allow communication across different social media platforms. It is emerging as a key part of the social media landscape that seeks to offer a more seamless experience and to improve the quality of interactions among online communities.


For more on the fediverse read this explainer, watch this video and see the kinds of communities that are appearing on the fediverse as alternatives to legacy social media platforms.

name: Resources: Tips for contacting experts
content:
Early in the project

Consult well-connected people who will open doors to others, in addition to being good sources of information themselves.

Write the letter you want someone else to send!

Use these tips to help you draft an email or letter that experts you turn to can easily forward to others by writing a draft you want them to forward.


  • Be brief - aim for no more than three short paragraphs.

  • Avoid - starting your email or letter with “My name is…” or “I”. You will sign off with your name and you want to indicate you are more interested in the recipient than yourself.

  • Get to the point quickly - state what your email or letter is about and what you want in your first paragraph. Busy people appreciate the time this saves them.

  • Be compelling - include a line about the problem you are trying to solve and why it matters.

  • Be specific - state clearly what you are asking for. If you are seeking an interview, include a few questions you would ask.

  • Keep your ask small - this makes it easier for the person to say ‘yes’ to your request, and chances are they will give you more once you have successfully engaged them.

  • Explain how you will use their input - people will want to know where and how their advice will be applied.

  • Re-read and revise - allow time to revise the letter or ask a colleague to review it to help you see it through the eyes of the recipient and what would help them to say ‘yes’ to your request.

Think carefully about who needs to be consulted

Ask yourself who may feel disrespected if you do not inform them of your work, consult with them, or invite them to an early meeting or discussion. Find ways to seek out the perspectives or advice of these people early on in your fast field scanning process. This may include key people inside your organization.

Busy and important people

Interview these people late in the process, once you have strong knowledge about your subject so you can make the most of what is likely to be the only opportunity you will have to speak with them.

name: Resources: Evidence clearinghouses
content:
Evidence clearinghouses collect and evaluate academic studies of policy interventions and are one of the most important sources of evidence for finding what works. Here are links to some clearinghouses you may find useful. We also welcome your further suggestions at <insert InnovateUS email contact>.


Multi-topic clearinghouses

  • Results First Clearinghouse Database

    Established with the support of The Pew Charitable Trusts and now operated by Penn State University, Results First catalogs and rates interventions on a spectrum from negative impact to positive impact. It covers interventions related to education, public and mental health, child and family well-being, employment and job training, crime and delinquency, substance use, and sexual behavior and teen pregnancy.

  • Campbell Collaboration

    The Campbell Collaboration is a social science research network which catalogs systematic reviews, develops 'evidence and gap maps' to visually represent the strength of evidence associated with specific interventions. It also produces research summaries and policy briefs. The Collaboration covers topics that include ageing, disability, education, children & young persons wellbeing, social welfare, crime and justice, and business and management.

  • Social Systems Evidence (SSE)

    SSE is an initiative of the McMaster Health Forum and the Monash Sustainable Development Institute (MSDI). It is a repository of research evidence syntheses related to a range of government sectors and program areas such as: climate action, community and social services, economic development and growth, education, environmental conservation, education, housing and transportation.

Topic-specific clearinghouses

  • Cochrane Library

    The Cochrane Library is a long standing and respected source of systematic evidence reviews in medicine and healthcare.

  • Health Systems Evidence (HSE)

    HSE is an initiative of the McMaster Health Forum which provides a repository of research evidence syntheses covering governance, financial and delivery arrangements within health systems.

  • What Works Clearinghouse (WWC)

    The WWC is an initiative of the Institute of Education Sciences (IES) within the U.S. Department of Education. It aims to provide scientific evidence on which to ground education practice and policy. It provides practice-guides, intervention reports, and reviews of individual studies that address school readiness and education from infancy through adulthood across a range of population groups. The WWC also offers training for those interested in becoming reviewers.

  • Pathways to Work Evidence Clearinghouse

    The Pathways to Work Evidence Clearinghouse focuses on systematic reviews of interventions that improve employment-related outcomes for populations with low incomes. It includes ‘evidence snapshots’, synthesis reports, and a series of YouTube videos that assist you to explore their materials.

  • Collaboration for Environmental Evidence Database of Evidence Reviews (CEEDER)

    CEEDER aims to help policy makers, managers, funders, and the general public to find reliable evidence reviews and syntheses to inform their decision making in environmental management. It catalogs and rates evidence reviews sourced from commercially published journals and gray literature sources.

  • Network for Business Sustainability (NBS)

    The NBS is a non-profit focused on sustainable development with six ‘expert knowledge hubs’: climate change, circular economy, sustainable finance, sustainable innovation, social justice and sustainable business education. It offers evidence-based content that draws on the research and experience of academics and managers in the network.

content:
The course conclusion summarizes the key learning points, including understanding GenAI, and mastering prompt engineering. Participants are encouraged to continue their learning journey through additional resources and courses on risk management and organizational AI deployment.

Got questions? Get in touch with us at hello@innovate-us.org.

Happy learning!

How to use: This transcript describes what is visible on screen that is not spoken aloud.

Congratulations!

You have completed the Using GenAI in Government course.

We have translated the complexity of AI into practical, easy-to-understand concepts and positioned you to

concretely incorporate GenAI into your day-to-day work.

We have discussed ways in which GenAI can generate original content and analyze large quantities of existing

data and information.

We have reviewed many concepts such as prompt engineering with examples and exercises, to enable you to effectively

deploy GenAI to address your organizational priorities.

Now, with a solid foundation, we are ready to look at the more challenging aspects of AI in the next

course in this series, Understanding Risk and Building Resilience.

As you have learned, AI is a powerful tool, but it comes with real risks.

In the next course, you will learn how to identify and mitigate those risks in your work.

Before you go, please take a moment to complete the course evaluation.

Your feedback helps us improve our courses and better support public professionals like you.

If you would like to explore further, check out the additional resources.

These resources include articles, toolkits, and guides to help you continue learning.

You can access them anytime, and we encourage you to share them with colleagues who may benefit.

We have also included some optional next steps and suggested resources for those who have completed this course.

Thank you for joining us in this course!

We look forward to seeing you in the next one.
